entities.name: Aulus Cornelius Palma Frontonianus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aulus Cornelius Palma Frontonianus, a distinguished Roman statesman and military commander, rose to significant prominence during the reigns of Emperors Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan. Twice holding the prestigious office of consul ordinarius, first in AD 99 alongside Quintus Sosius Senecio and again in 109 with Publius Calvisius Tullus Ruso, Palma's career marked a period of robust imperial expansion. His strategic importance is primarily tied to his role as the architect of Rome's annexation of the Nabataean Kingdom, transforming it into the province of Arabia Petraea, a pivotal moment in the consolidation of Roman power in the Near East.

Palma's most celebrated achievement occurred during his governorship of Syria, a post he likely held from around 104 to 108 CE. From this strategic base, he spearheaded the Roman invasion of the Nabataean Kingdom in 106 CE. This swift and decisive military campaign resulted in the subjugation of the Nabataeans, whose capital Petra had long been a crucial hub for trade routes connecting the Mediterranean with Arabia and India. The formal annexation established Arabia Petraea as a new Roman province, with Bostra designated as its capital, significantly extending Rome's eastern frontier and securing vital commercial arteries for the empire. His successes were instrumental in furthering Emperor Trajan's expansionist vision, earning him high honors, including triumphal ornaments.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Aulus Cornelius Palma Frontonianus's conquest and annexation of the Nabataean Kingdom in 106 CE fundamentally reshaped the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, establishing the strategically vital province of Arabia Petraea. This act significantly expanded Roman control over major trade routes, leaving a permanent mark on the region's political geography and economic integration into the empire.
